doc.title: Kenny Davern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Singing through the horn: why modern players bore him
summary: Rowe quotes Davern's earlier remark about melody; Davern says embellishing players bore him and cites Armstrong and Caruso as masters of one note.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: I had something I noticed in your last interview, I thought I would just start with this. You had said, talking about a person’s, the way they play and improvising a solo and so forth, “what it boils down to is can you sing through your horn. Can you sustain a melody and make it beautiful without all the gibberish and nonsense and trying to show everybody how many notes you can play around a melodic theme. Can you state simply the bare essentials of a melody and make it convincing.”
You said that. Do you have a problem with any of the more modern players who don’t seem to—
They embellish on the actual simplicity of making a statement, a melodic statement, as devoid of superfluous things, notes, gimmicks. Yeah I have a problem with them, sure. They bore me.

Because Louis Armstrong was probably the greatest exponent of being able to play one note and making it more meaning, with a great deal of energy. It’s getting that karma going on that note. Caruso could do it too. And maybe a few others but not many it seems.
